subcomponents.title: Maintains clear boundaries and scope discipline

criteria.rationale: The demo has clear boundaries. The registry (presentations/index.ts) holds only slug, title and a lazy `load`. Talk.tsx only composes `Presentation`. steps.ts only maps modules to kit `Step`s, and modules.ts only aggregates the nine step files. Each step file exports `meta` and `entities()`. entities.ts holds only ids, layout.ts only geometry, and cards.tsx the shared card and link builders. SampleScene.tsx is the single Scene, and talk.css holds the presentation-local styling. I traced the shared constants and public inputs to rendered consumers and found none dead. Every `E` member and every `R` member is used by a step module or cards.tsx. `CARD_X`, `CARD_Y`, `CARD_W`, `CARD_H`, `card` and `part` are used by cards.tsx and 08-loop.tsx. `SamplePayload.upTo` is consumed by SampleScene and steps.ts. The `title` prop is not ignored. Talk.tsx passes it, `Presentation` destructures it, and the root element consumes it as `data-presentation-title-text={title}`. The per-step visible titles come from `step.title` in Footer, which is a separate contract. layout.ts imports the `Rect` type directly from `nodes/common.ts` rather than the barrel, which is a minor style matter and not a boundary violation.

criteria.rationale: Newcomer entry is delayed by the continuing layout duration and applies to the entry only. In constants.ts, LAYOUT_T = 0.6 and ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T. Appear starts at opacity 0 and animates to 1 with delay ENTER_DELAY (default) and duration ENTER_T. The kit's entity primitives (Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame, and Arrow's line) move with a layout transition of duration LAYOUT_T and no delay. So persisting entities move immediately, and the newcomer's visible entry starts at 0.6s, when the layout move ends. The delay is not applied to layout motion. Appear is keyed and stays mounted for an entity's lifetime, so continuing entities are not re-faded. I read every sample step module (01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09), plus cards.tsx, entities.ts and modules.ts. criteria.rationale: All three clauses are met. (1) Bounded readiness: `startPreview` in both common.mjs copies sets `deadline = Date.now() + 20000`. criteria.rationale: The delivered tests that drive a real browser are the three integration suites: inspect.int.test.ts, verify.e2e.test.ts and bootstrap.int.test.ts. None of them sleeps for a fixed time before asserting. Each one launches verify or inspect through `exec()` in helpers.ts. That promise resolves only on the child's 'close' event (helpers.ts:46-55), which is observable process state. The tests then assert on the exit code, the output and the files written. The one wait loop in a test is `gone(pid)` (helpers.ts:66-74). It polls `alive(pid)` against a deadline and returns as soon as the state changes, so it is a polling wait. Every fixed timer in the test tree serves another purpose. inspect.int.test.ts:64 is inside a generated fixture Scene's useEffect and simulates content that settles late in the app under test; no test waits on it. verify-script.test.ts:165 is inside a fake-page stub's `goto`, which makes a fake error arrive late; no browser is involved. In inspect-script.test.ts:159-162, `sleep` is an injected fake that only records events and advances a fake clock. A grep for setTimeout, waitForTimeout and sleep across tests/ and src/**/*.test.* finds only these occurrences and the gone() poll. The jsdom component tests wait on DOM state with `waitFor` and `findByText` (Stage.test.tsx:65-76, Router.test.tsx:38-48). No test treats an immediate call such as reading an element count as a wait. Judge A (pass) and Judge B (pass) are consistent with this source. Judge C (fail) points out that verify's renderSteps and inspect's captureSteps wait a fixed settle interval inside the scripts. Those delays belong to the verification scripts under test, not to the tests. The criterion asks whether the browser tests sleep instead of waiting for state. These tests wait on child-process close and poll process liveness, and none waits a fixed time before asserting. The `--settle-ms 50` in inspect.int.test.ts:123 is an argument passed to the script under test, not a sleep in the test. The review guidance also says longer fixed settle delays earn neither credit nor failure. Judge C's reason therefore does not decide the requirement.

votes.rationale: Grouping: steps.ts gives all nine steps `groupKey: 'how-to-make-a-presentation'` and `Scene: SampleScene`. Stage.tsx keys its single `motion.div` by `step.groupKey ?? step.id`, so one scene instance stays mounted across all nine steps and only `payload.upTo` changes. Identity: entities.ts defines the presentation-owned `E` ids under the `htmp/` namespace. Every step module and cards.tsx passes these as `id` to the kit nodes (Box, Label, Arrow, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame). Each node forwards `id` to Motion as `layoutId={id}` and `data-presentation-entity={id}`, with `layout` set on the non-Arrow nodes. SampleScene returns the cumulative `slice(0, upTo)` of all nine modules' entities, so each entity keeps the same id and a stable React key at every later step. Arrow does not set `layout`, but it carries `layoutId`, and its line `animate`s `x1..y2` to the new endpoints. I traced every `E` member to a rendered element's `id`: you, prompt, skill, converse, question and tray; card, part, link and morph via cards.tsx; ghost, ghostLabel and depth; socket and socketLabel; verify, verifyLabel, verifyLink and pass; modify, modifyLabel, flag and flagLabel; reveal and revealLabel. None is dead. The `${E.you}-label` and `${E.skill}-label` nested labels also get ids. sample.test.tsx confirms this with a DOM-node-survival test: the `htmp/you` node and the step wrapper are the same DOM nodes after four ArrowRight presses. It also asserts one shared groupKey and unique keys and ids. groupKey preserves the scene mount, while the E-derived layoutIds preserve entity identity.

votes.rationale: The demo has clear boundaries. The registry (presentations/index.ts) holds only slug, title and a lazy `load`. Talk.tsx only composes `Presentation`. steps.ts only maps modules to kit `Step`s, and modules.ts only aggregates the nine step files. Each step file exports `meta` and `entities()`. entities.ts holds only ids, layout.ts only geometry, and cards.tsx the shared card and link builders. SampleScene.tsx is the single Scene, and talk.css holds the presentation-local styling. I traced the shared constants and public inputs to rendered consumers and found none dead. Every `E` member and every `R` member is used by a step module or cards.tsx. `CARD_X`, `CARD_Y`, `CARD_W`, `CARD_H`, `card` and `part` are used by cards.tsx and 08-loop.tsx. `SamplePayload.upTo` is consumed by SampleScene and steps.ts. The `title` prop is not ignored. Talk.tsx passes it, `Presentation` destructures it, and the root element consumes it as `data-presentation-title-text={title}`. The per-step visible titles come from `step.title` in Footer, which is a separate contract. layout.ts imports the `Rect` type directly from `nodes/common.ts` rather than the barrel, which is a minor style matter and not a boundary violation.

votes.rationale: The chrome sets a semantic current-state attribute together with a stable active hook. Footer.tsx's progress dots set `aria-current='step'` and `data-presentation-active='true'` on the active step. Toc.tsx's entries do the same for the active era. The presentation-owned talk.css gives the active state a visible style. `[data-presentation-progress-dot][data-presentation-active='true']` gets an accent background, border and `scale(1.35)`. `[data-presentation-toc-entry][data-presentation-active='true']` gets a panel background, accent border, ink color and bold weight. votes.rationale: startPreview reserves an ephemeral port with freePort(), which closes the probe server before use. It starts vite with --strictPort. Readiness then comes from HTTP polling of `${origin}/`. The only ownership check is `child.exitCode !== null`, sampled at the top of each loop iteration before the fetch. It is not raced against the child's exit, and readiness is not taken from the child's own announcement. If another process grabs the released port, it can answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. The guidance calls strictPort plus liveness sampled before each request insufficient.

votes.rationale: startPreview reserves a free port with freePort(), which listens on port 0, reads the port, and closes the server. It then starts vite preview with --strictPort. Readiness comes only from HTTP fetch polling of that address. Ownership of the spawned child is checked only through `if (child.exitCode !== null)` at the top of each loop iteration, before the next request. The code never takes readiness from the child's own announced address. It never races the poll against the child's exit event. If another server answers on the port before the child's exit is observed, the poll succeeds. The port is released before the child binds, so a different process can take it in between. demo-integration.rationale: Talk.tsx renders the kit's `Presentation` with steps, title, initialMode and className. steps.ts builds `Step<SamplePayload>` objects with groupKey, Scene and payload. Stage.tsx mounts `step.Scene` with the payload. SampleScene.tsx is typed with the kit's `SceneProps`, renders `SceneLayer`, and the step modules build entities from kit nodes wrapped in `Appear`, all imported through the kit barrel. The demo has no navigation, fit-scale or morph logic of its own. This meets the Talk and shared Scene boundary requirement.
evidence: Talk.tsx: `<Presentation steps={STEPS} title=... initialMode="browse" className="htmp" />`
steps.ts: `STEP_MODULES.map((m,i)=>({...m.meta, groupKey, Scene: SampleScene, payload:{upTo:i+1}}))`
SampleScene.tsx: `<SceneLayer>{STEP_MODULES.slice(0, payload.upTo).flatMap(m => m.entities())}</SceneLayer>`

votes.rationale: startPreview reserves an ephemeral port with freePort(), which closes the probe server before use. It starts vite with --strictPort. Readiness then comes from HTTP polling of `${origin}/`. The only ownership check is `child.exitCode !== null`, sampled at the top of each loop iteration before the fetch. It is not raced against the child's exit, and readiness is not taken from the child's own announcement. If another process grabs the released port, it can answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. The guidance calls strictPort plus liveness sampled before each request insufficient.

votes.rationale: startPreview reserves a free port with freePort(), which listens on port 0, reads the port, and closes the server. It then starts vite preview with --strictPort. Readiness comes only from HTTP fetch polling of that address. Ownership of the spawned child is checked only through `if (child.exitCode !== null)` at the top of each loop iteration, before the next request. The code never takes readiness from the child's own announced address. It never races the poll against the child's exit event. If another server answers on the port before the child's exit is observed, the poll succeeds. The port is released before the child binds, so a different process can take it in between. The guidance names this pattern, liveness sampled before each request with readiness from HTTP polling, as a fail. A strict port alone is also insufficient.

It also says to fail when the transition check turns a non-numeric hook into a number that still passes its comparison, giving Number(null) === 0 on the first step as the example. In scripts/verify.mjs, readStep finds the root with document.querySelector('[data-step-index]'). That selector matches an element whose attribute is present but empty. readStep then sets index to Number(root.getAttribute('data-step-index')), and Number('') is 0. The first-step check on line 108 accepts `observed.index === 0` with no check that the hook holds a real number. So an empty, non-numeric data-step-index on step 1 passes the first-step comparison. Judges A and C are correct about two other cases: an element with no attribute makes readStep return null, and a non-numeric string gives NaN, so both fail strict equality. Their count reasoning (a missing or empty count does not equal 9) is also correct. None of that covers the empty-attribute case: it matches the selector, becomes 0 and satisfies `observed.index === 0`. The stalled-transition e2e test and the unit test checkTransition(2, 3, null) cover later steps and null values only, so they do not rule this out. The comparison therefore accepts a non-numeric hook as a valid first-step index, which is the failure the guidance names.

The cited loop does have a timeout on the readiness wait, though. C's point depends on a server that accepts the connection but never answers. The candidate does not produce that scenario and the review guidance does not name it. So C's observation does not show an unbounded readiness wait, and the criterion's 'every wait for preview readiness has a timeout' clause is met.

first_results.rationale: The delivered tests that start a browser are the integration tests (verify.e2e, inspect.int and bootstrap.int). Each spawns the verify or inspect script through `exec`, which resolves only on the child's `close` event, and then asserts on the exit code, output and written files. None of them calls a fixed sleep or waitForTimeout before asserting. The only wait in the tests is `gone(pid)` in helpers.ts. It polls `alive(pid)` against a deadline, so it waits on observable process state rather than sleeping for a fixed time. The jsdom component tests use testing-library `waitFor`, which is an auto-waiting assertion on DOM state. The setTimeout at inspect.int.test.ts:64 is inside a generated fixture scene, and the one in verify-script.test.ts:165 is inside a fake page stub; neither is a test waiting before an assertion. I rule A and B's pass. Judge C fails the criterion because `STEP_SETTLE_MS` in verify.mjs and `settleMs` in inspect add fixed settle delays. Those delays live in the delivered verification and inspection tools, which the criterion does not judge. Even there they come after a polling `waitForFunction` on the step index. The tests themselves still wait for process completion and observable state. The guidance also lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. So C's reason does not show that any browser test sleeps for a fixed time instead of waiting for state.

first_results.rationale: The requirement asks two things. First, the candidate must record the revision it last tested. Second, that revision must be the final revision, or the final revision must have no product changes since it. The last acceptance pass is round 2, recorded in a verified exploration log and in the verified final handoff. Both name the tested head as c26e4c9f9c2ec64787f9c9a2f8cc7c8722572064. The handoff says the local tested HEAD and the final PR head match. The runner's gate notice independently gives local HEAD as the same SHA. The last tested revision is therefore the final revision. Round 2 was a scoped pass against declared base 85feb04. It records that the only product change in that range was skills/presentation/scripts/scaffold.mjs. That file's changed traversal code was exercised directly: detect runs on the prior type-only fixture, the vendor-first fixture, the comment fixture and the unquoted-HTML fixture, plus production builds and the project-local inspect helper. The command logs are included. The harness lists 12 product files changed since the archived round-0 SHA 9185313. All of them were exercised by the verified round-1 pass at 85feb04 or the round-2 pass: - Stage.tsx and canvasPoint.ts: narrow and wide motion traces, plus a resize-then-reverse trace. - verify.mjs and common.mjs: the symlinked verify run on a renamed registry and the late-error verify run. - inspect-presentation.mjs: inspect runs in rounds 1 and 2. - SKILL.md: the skill-directed host wiring in R3. - scaffold.mjs: the symlinked apply, the host apply and the barrel detect. - The five template copies count as explored through the harness mirror groups. Judges A and B fail the criterion because the only verified tested-revision artifact names 9185313, and because the harness reports 'final-revision-not-established'. That artifact is the archived file output/acceptance-round0/acceptance-tested-revision.txt, a round-0 history record. It is not the candidate's record of its last tested revision. The harness findings are computed from that archived file alone. The criterion says to use the harness facts together with verified candidate records, and the verified round-2 log and handoff do record the final SHA as tested. Their reason therefore does not show that any clause of the requirement is unmet.

results.rationale: The requirement asks two things. First, the candidate must record the revision it last tested. Second, that revision must be the final revision, or the final revision must have no product changes since it. The last acceptance pass is round 2, recorded in a verified exploration log and in the verified final handoff. Both name the tested head as c26e4c9f9c2ec64787f9c9a2f8cc7c8722572064. The handoff says the local tested HEAD and the final PR head match. The runner's gate notice independently gives local HEAD as the same SHA. The last tested revision is therefore the final revision. Round 2 was a scoped pass against declared base 85feb04. It records that the only product change in that range was skills/presentation/scripts/scaffold.mjs. That file's changed traversal code was exercised directly: detect runs on the prior type-only fixture, the vendor-first fixture, the comment fixture and the unquoted-HTML fixture, plus production builds and the project-local inspect helper. The command logs are included. The harness lists 12 product files changed since the archived round-0 SHA 9185313. All of them were exercised by the verified round-1 pass at 85feb04 or the round-2 pass: - Stage.tsx and canvasPoint.ts: narrow and wide motion traces, plus a resize-then-reverse trace. - verify.mjs and common.mjs: the symlinked verify run on a renamed registry and the late-error verify run. - inspect-presentation.mjs: inspect runs in rounds 1 and 2. - SKILL.md: the skill-directed host wiring in R3. - scaffold.mjs: the symlinked apply, the host apply and the barrel detect. - The five template copies count as explored through the harness mirror groups. Judges A and B fail the criterion because the only verified tested-revision artifact names 9185313, and because the harness reports 'final-revision-not-established'. That artifact is the archived file output/acceptance-round0/acceptance-tested-revision.txt, a round-0 history record. It is not the candidate's record of its last tested revision. The harness findings are computed from that archived file alone. The criterion says to use the harness facts together with verified candidate records, and the verified round-2 log and handoff do record the final SHA as tested. Their reason therefore does not show that any clause of the requirement is unmet.

demo-integration.rationale: The auditor's argument is that writing the title to a data attribute counts as consuming it, even if nothing reads the attribute. The guidance asks for the title to be traced through the demo, and the check fails if the public title contract is ignored rather than consumed. The supplied source shows that Talk passes the title. Presentation then writes it only to `data-presentation-title-text` on the root div. The material shows no other use of the title. It is not rendered as visible text, not set as the document title, and not used as an accessible name. Header shows only the brand, the step number and the era. Footer's h2 shows `step.title`, not the presentation title. A value that ends up only in a non-semantic data attribute has no visible or functional effect. Under the plain meaning of a presentation title, that is ignored, not consumed. A data attribute alone does not meet the title contract. The auditor's other point, that the rest of the code is well organised, does not answer this specific reason for the fail.
evidence: Presentation.tsx declares `title?: string` and destructures it. Its only use is `data-presentation-title-text={title}` on the root div.
Footer.tsx renders `<h2 data-presentation-title="">{step.title}</h2>`. This is the per-step title, not the presentation title.
Header.tsx renders the brand, the step number and `step.era`. It never receives or renders the presentation title.
Talk.tsx passes `title="How to Use This Skill to Make a Presentation"`. In the supplied material, that value never becomes visible or accessible output.

candidate_reported_ci.verbatim: - **Rationale:** This makes the outcome unambiguous for automation and satisfies "identifying which check failed".

- **Requirement:** presentation-skill, "Self-bootstrapping scaffold" / "Partial scaffold" (scaffold only the missing anchors and their dependencies, without disturbing present ones) and "Self-verify before reporting completion". Presentation-verification, "Pass/fail reporting" (a clear outcome identifying which check failed) and "Missing sample fails". Test plan, INT-001 (the materialized app passes its local verification entry point).

- **Recommended integration test (not added this round):** a browser-backed test that loads a registered fixture with a moving continuing entity at a narrow viewport and asserts the first animated frame stays within a few pixels of the pre-transition position. I did not add it because integration suites may not be run in this step and an unrun browser test could fail CI. It belongs in the next round's integration suite.
